title: Checkpoint 6 Science — Practice Test 2

summary: A full two-paper practice test in Checkpoint style (2 × 35 minutes, 2 × 40 marks), with automatic marking and a full mark scheme. By Mohamed Abdelkriem.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: This is a full practice test for Cambridge Primary Checkpoint Science (0097): two papers that cover the whole Stage 6 curriculum.
Biology: the heart and blood (6Bs.01), the lungs (6Bs.02), growing up (6Bs.03, 6Bp.01), diseases, hygiene and defences (6Bp.02, 6Bp.03, 6Bp.04), food webs, toxins and energy (6Be.01, 6Be.02, 6Be.03)
Chemistry: melting and boiling points, gases, conductors (6Cp.01, 6Cp.02, 6Cp.03); reversible changes, dissolving, boiling and evaporation, chemical reactions (6Cc.01 to 6Cc.05)
Physics: mass, weight and gravity, force diagrams, forces and motion, floating and sinking (6Pf.01 to 6Pf.05); reflection and refraction (6Ps.01, 6Ps.02); circuits (6Pe.01, 6Pe.02)
Earth and space: rocks, fossils and soil (6ESp.01 to 6ESp.04); the rock cycle (6ESc.01); the Solar System and the Moon (6ESs.01, 6ESs.02)
Thinking and Working Scientifically: variables, fair tests, anomalous results, means, patterns, predictions, graphs and conclusions

**What this is:** a complete practice test written in the style of the Cambridge Primary Checkpoint Science test (0097), taken at the end of Stage 6. Every question is new; the contexts are a family kitchen, a football match, a farm in the Nile Delta, a playground, a night sky observation log and a model boat competition.
**Two papers, like the real test:** Paper 1 — **35 minutes, 40 marks**. Paper 2 — **35 minutes, 40 marks**. That is 80 marks in total. The timer here runs for 35 minutes for each paper.
**Calculator:** the cover of the real Paper 1 says "You may use a calculator." For Paper 2, check with your teacher. The numbers in this test are small, so you can also work them out by hand.
**Equipment:** a black or dark blue pen, an HB pencil for diagrams and graphs, a ruler and a calculator. In the real test you answer on the question paper, and no extra materials are needed.
**Write on paper first if you like.** You can also print the question paper (PDF link above the questions) and do it like a real exam, then type your answers in.
**Look at the marks:** [1] = one point; [2] = two separate points, or a point and a reason. Give one answer only — a wrong answer next to a right one loses the mark.

**How marking works here:** answers you type (a word, a letter, a number) or choose (multiple choice) are **checked automatically**. Written explanations are **marked by you**: when you finish, compare your answer with the mark scheme shown and give yourself the marks you really earned. Be strict, like an examiner.
**Your score is a practice score only.** It shows your strengths and weaknesses; it is not an official Cambridge result.

Karim plays in a school football match. The diagram is a simple model of how blood travels around his body. The arrows show the direction in which the blood flows. A, B, C and D are blood vessels.
questions.q: (c) In Karim's leg muscles, blood flows through very narrow blood vessels with walls only one cell thick. Name these blood vessels.
questions.e: **Capillaries.** Their very thin walls let oxygen and nutrients pass out of the blood into the muscle cells, and let waste such as carbon dioxide pass back into the blood.

Question 1
Karim plays in a school football match. The diagram is a simple model of how blood travels around his body. The arrows show the direction in which the blood flows. A, B, C and D are blood vessels.
questions.q: (d) Which sentence describes the job of Karim's circulatory system?
c: It breaks down his food into small pieces.
It moves the bones in his legs when he runs.
It carries oxygen, nutrients and waste around his body.
It takes air into his body and lets air out.
questions.e: The circulatory system (heart, blood vessels and blood) **transports** oxygen, nutrients and waste. Breaking down food is the digestive system, moving bones is muscles and the skeleton, and taking air in and out is the respiratory system.

Question 2
Karim wears a heart-rate watch. He plays football for the first 40 minutes, then sits and rests on the bench from 40 to 60 minutes. The graph shows his heart rate.
questions.q: (c) Explain why Karim's heart rate increased while he was playing football.
questions.ms: 1 mark: his muscles need more oxygen / more energy / more nutrients (glucose) when he exercises. 1 mark: the heart beats faster to pump blood faster, so more oxygen (and nutrients) reach the muscles / more carbon dioxide (waste) is taken away. Do not accept 'he is tired' or 'his heart is working hard' with no reason.
questions.e: Model answer: "When Karim runs, his **muscles need more oxygen** (and nutrients) to release energy. His heart beats faster so that blood carrying oxygen is **pumped to the muscles more quickly**, and carbon dioxide is taken away faster." Two separate ideas are needed for 2 marks: the need (more oxygen) and the job of the faster heart beat (delivering it).

questions.p:
Question 3
Mum is cooking dinner in the family kitchen. She cuts up raw chicken and then makes a salad.
questions.q: (a) Raw chicken can carry harmful bacteria. Which action is best for stopping these bacteria from getting into the salad?
c: Use the same knife for the chicken and the salad, but cut the salad quickly.
Leave the salad on the worktop near the chicken for a few hours.
Rinse the chicken in the sink next to the salad bowl.
Wash the board, the knife and her hands with hot soapy water after cutting the chicken.
questions.e: Washing the board, knife and hands with hot soapy water removes and kills the bacteria, so they are not passed to food that will not be cooked. The other actions all help bacteria spread or grow.

questions.p:
Question 3
Mum is cooking dinner in the family kitchen. She cuts up raw chicken and then makes a salad.
questions.q: (b) If a few bacteria are swallowed with food, most of them are killed in the stomach. Name the substance in the stomach that kills them.
questions.e: **Stomach acid** (hydrochloric acid) kills most pathogens that we swallow. It is one of the body's defences, together with the skin and mucus.

Question 3
Mum is cooking dinner in the family kitchen. She cuts up raw chicken and then makes a salad.
questions.q: (c) In summer the family leaves the kitchen window open at night and mosquitoes fly in. Some mosquitoes can carry pathogens from one person to another. Give **two** ways the family can avoid being bitten by mosquitoes.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, any two: put a net/screen on the window or close the window at dusk; sleep under a mosquito net; use insect repellent (cream/spray) on the skin; wear long sleeves and long trousers in the evening; empty standing water (buckets, plant pots) where mosquitoes breed; use a plug-in mosquito repellent/insect spray in the room. Do not accept 'wash hands' or 'cook food well' (these do not stop bites).
questions.e: Example answer: "1. Put a net (screen) over the window. 2. Spray insect repellent on their skin before sleeping." A mosquito that carries a pathogen is called a **vector**; stopping the bite stops the pathogen from passing between hosts.

questions.q: (d) The farmer puts out rat poison. The poison is toxic and stays inside the bodies of animals that take it in. A few weeks later, an owl on the farm is found dead. Explain how the poison got into the owl's body.
questions.ms: 1 mark: rats eat the poison (the poison is in the rats' bodies). 1 mark: the owl eats (many) poisoned rats / eats snakes that ate poisoned rats, so the poison passes along the food chain (and builds up in the owl). Do not accept 'the owl ate the poison' with no link to the rats.
questions.e: Model answer: "The **rats ate the poison**, and it stayed in their bodies. The **owl ate the poisoned rats** (and snakes that had eaten poisoned rats), so the poison passed along the food chain into the owl." Because an owl eats many rats, the poison builds up to a large amount in its body.

questions.q: (e) Name the original source of the energy for every food chain in this food web.

Salma mixes lemon juice with baking soda in a glass in the kitchen. The mixture fizzes. She puts a thermometer in the mixture.
temperature at the start = 22 °C
temperature after 1 minute = 17 °C
The word equation for the reaction is:
citric acid + sodium hydrogencarbonate → sodium citrate + water + carbon dioxide
questions.q: (b) Give **one other** observation that shows a chemical reaction is happening.
questions.ms: 1 mark: fizzing / bubbles / a gas is produced (accept: carbon dioxide is given off). Do not accept 'the temperature changed' (already given) or 'it dissolves'.
questions.e: **The mixture fizzes — bubbles of gas are made.** A gas being produced is evidence of a chemical reaction. (The gas is carbon dioxide, a product in the word equation.)

temperature at the start = 22 °C
temperature after 1 minute = 17 °C
The word equation for the reaction is:

questions.q: (c) How many **reactants** are there in this reaction?
questions.e: Reactants are the substances on the **left** of the arrow, the ones that react: citric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate. That is **2**. The three substances on the right are products (new substances).

temperature at the start = 22 °C

The word equation for the reaction is:

questions.q: (d) Salma also cooks dinner. Which of these changes is **reversible**?
c: melting butter in a warm pan
frying an egg
toasting bread
baking a cake
questions.e: Melted butter turns back into solid butter when it cools, so **melting butter** is a reversible (physical) change. Frying an egg, toasting bread and baking a cake make new substances, so they cannot be reversed.

Youssef investigates friction on the playground slide. He sticks a different material to the bottom of the same wooden block, lets the block go from the top of the slide and measures the time it takes to reach the bottom. He does each test three times.
Material on the block | Test 1 time in s | Test 2 time in s | Test 3 time in s | Mean time in s
plastic | 2.1 | 2.3 | 2.2 | 2.2
cotton cloth | 2.8 | 2.9 | 3.0 | 2.9
carpet | 4.6 | 3.5 | 4.8 | ?
sandpaper | 6.2 | 6.0 | 6.4 | 6.2
questions.q: (a) Which is the **independent** variable in Youssef's investigation (the variable he changes)?
c: the time taken to reach the bottom
the material on the bottom of the block
the length of the slide
the mass of the block

questions.q: (f) Write a conclusion for Youssef's investigation. Use your scientific knowledge to explain it.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the rougher the material, the longer the time / sandpaper took longest and plastic took the shortest time (a correct pattern from the results). 1 mark: rougher materials make more friction, which acts against the movement (opposite to the direction of motion) and slows the block down. questions.e: Model answer: "The **rougher** the material, the **longer** the block took to slide down: plastic was fastest (2.2 s) and sandpaper slowest (6.2 s). This is because a rougher surface makes **more friction** between the block and the slide. Friction acts **against the movement**, so it slows the block down more."

questions.p:
Question 8
The family kitchen has a granite worktop, a marble floor and a sandstone wall tile.
questions.q: (a) Granite is made of large crystals that fit tightly together. It formed when hot liquid rock cooled slowly underground. What type of rock is granite?
questions.e: Rock that forms when magma (liquid rock) cools and **solidifies** is **igneous** rock. Its crystals fit tightly together; slow cooling underground makes large crystals.

questions.p:
Question 8
The family kitchen has a granite worktop, a marble floor and a sandstone wall tile.
questions.q: (b) Marble is a metamorphic rock. How did the marble form?
c: Sand grains were stuck together in layers under the sea.
Lava cooled quickly on the surface of the Earth.
Pieces of rock were carried away by a river.
Limestone was heated and squeezed deep underground, without melting.
questions.e: Metamorphic rock forms when an existing rock is changed by **heat and pressure** deep underground **without melting**. Marble forms from limestone in this way (metamorphism). Option A describes sedimentary rock and option B describes igneous rock.

questions.p:
Question 8
The family kitchen has a granite worktop, a marble floor and a sandstone wall tile.
questions.q: (c) The sandstone tile has a fossil of a small sea shell in it. Describe how this fossil formed in sedimentary rock.
questions.ms: Any two, 1 mark each: the animal died and fell to the sea bed / bottom of the water; it was quickly covered (buried) by sand / sediment; more layers of sediment built up on top and pressed the lower layers into rock (sandstone); the shell (hard part) was replaced by minerals / left its shape (a mould or cast) in the rock. Do not accept 'the shell melted into the rock'.
questions.e: Model answer: "The sea animal **died** and its shell sank to the sea bed. It was **covered by sand** (sediment). More layers built up on top, and over a very long time the weight **pressed the sand into sandstone**. The shell was slowly **replaced by minerals**, which kept its shape as a fossil." Fossils form in sedimentary rock because the sediment buries the remains gently, without the heat that melts igneous rock.

questions.p:
Question 9
Laila keeps a night sky observation log. Every week she draws the Moon as she sees it from her balcony in Egypt.
questions.q: (b) About one week after 23 October, Laila cannot see the Moon at all. What is this phase of the Moon called?
questions.e: When the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun, its lit side faces away from us and we cannot see it: this is a **new Moon**. The cycle from one new Moon to the next takes about a month (about 29.5 days).

questions.p:
Question 9
Laila keeps a night sky observation log. Every week she draws the Moon as she sees it from her balcony in Egypt.
questions.q: (c) From 2 October to 16 October, the lit part of the Moon that Laila sees gets bigger. Explain why.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the Moon does not make its own light; it reflects light from the Sun / half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun. 1 mark: as the Moon moves round (orbits) the Earth, we see more of the lit half from Earth (until full Moon, when we see all of the lit half). Do not accept 'the Earth's shadow covers the Moon' or 'the Moon grows'.
questions.e: Model answer: "The Sun **always lights up half** of the Moon, and we see the Moon because it **reflects** sunlight. As the Moon **orbits the Earth**, we see a different amount of the lit half. From 2 to 16 October, more and more of the lit half faces the Earth, until at full Moon we see all of it." A common mistake is to say the Earth's shadow causes the phases — it does not.

questions.p:
Question 1
This question is about growing up.
questions.q: (a) Which change happens to **both** boys and girls during puberty?
c: The voice becomes much deeper.
Hair grows under the arms.
Breasts develop.
The shoulders become much wider.
questions.e: **Hair grows under the arms** (and in the pubic area) in both boys and girls. Other changes for both: a growth spurt, more sweat and oily skin. A much deeper voice and much wider shoulders happen in boys; breasts develop in girls.

questions.q: (b) Name the organs in the female reproductive system that make egg cells.
questions.e: The **ovaries** (there are two) make and release egg cells.

questions.p:
Question 2
Ahmed kicks a football high into the air during a match. The diagram shows the ball at the top of its path, when it is moving to the right. The arrows A, B, C and D are possible forces.
questions.q: (c) Later, the goalkeeper catches a ball that is moving towards him. Describe the effect of the force from his hands on the ball.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the force acts against the movement / in the opposite direction, so it slows the ball down and stops it. Accept: changes the ball's speed so it stops. Do not accept 'it makes the ball go faster'.
questions.e: The goalkeeper's hands push **against the direction of movement**, so the force **slows the ball down until it stops**. A force on a moving object can speed it up, slow it down or change its direction.

questions.p:
Question 2
Ahmed kicks a football high into the air during a match. The diagram shows the ball at the top of its path, when it is moving to the right. The arrows A, B, C and D are possible forces.
questions.q: (d) Ahmed breathes faster during the match. Which sentence describes what happens in his lungs?
c: Oxygen moves from his blood into the air in his lungs.
Carbon dioxide moves from the air in his lungs into his blood.
Food moves from the air in his lungs into his blood.
Oxygen moves from the air in his lungs into his blood.
questions.e: In the air sacs of the lungs, **oxygen moves from the air into the blood**, and carbon dioxide moves the other way (from the blood into the air, to be breathed out). Many other vertebrates, such as cats and birds, have lungs that work in a similar way.

questions.p:
Question 3
Mona plays in the playground. Her mass is 35 kg. On Earth, gravity is 10 N/kg.
questions.q: (a) Calculate Mona's weight on Earth.
questions.e: Weight = mass × gravity = 35 kg × 10 N/kg = **350 N**. Weight is a force, so it is measured in newtons (N).

questions.p:
Question 3
Mona plays in the playground. Her mass is 35 kg. On Earth, gravity is 10 N/kg.
questions.q: (b) Mona imagines playing on the Moon, where gravity is about 1.6 N/kg. Which sentence about Mona on the Moon is correct?
c: Her mass is still 35 kg, but her weight is less than 350 N.
Her mass is less than 35 kg, but her weight is still 350 N.
Her mass and her weight are both less than on Earth.
Her mass and her weight are both the same as on Earth.
questions.e: Mass (the amount of matter, in kg) does **not** change from place to place, so it is still 35 kg. Gravity is weaker on the Moon, so her **weight is less**: 35 × 1.6 = 56 N.

Depth of boat in cm | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.0 | ? | 3.0
questions.q: (a) Which is the **independent** variable in this investigation?
c: the depth of the boat in the water
the size of the water tank
the mass of the cargo
the shape of the boat
questions.e: The team changes the **mass of the cargo** on purpose, so it is the independent variable. The depth is what they measure (dependent). The boat's shape and the tank stay the same (control variables).

Question 4
At a model boat competition, Omar's team tests how the mass of cargo affects how deep their boat sits in the water. They measure the depth of the bottom of the boat below the water surface.
Mass of cargo in g | 0 | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80
Depth of boat in cm | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.0 | ? | 3.0
questions.q: (b) Describe the pattern in the results.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the greater the mass of cargo, the deeper the boat sits (lower in the water). Accept: depth goes up by 0.5 cm for every 20 g. Do not accept 'the depth changes' (no direction).
questions.e: **As the mass of the cargo increases, the boat sits deeper in the water.** In fact, every extra 20 g makes it sit 0.5 cm deeper.

questions.p:
Question 4
At a model boat competition, Omar's team tests how the mass of cargo affects how deep their boat sits in the water. They measure the depth of the bottom of the boat below the water surface.
Mass of cargo in g | 0 | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80
Depth of boat in cm | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.0 | ? | 3.0
questions.q: (c) Use the pattern to predict the depth of the boat when it carries 60 g of cargo.
questions.e: Each 20 g adds 0.5 cm. 40 g → 2.0 cm, so 60 g → 2.0 + 0.5 = **2.5 cm**. This also fits halfway between 2.0 cm (40 g) and 3.0 cm (80 g).

Question 4
At a model boat competition, Omar's team tests how the mass of cargo affects how deep their boat sits in the water. They measure the depth of the bottom of the boat below the water surface.
Mass of cargo in g | 0 | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80
Depth of boat in cm | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.0 | ? | 3.0
questions.q: (d) Another team rolls the same mass of modelling clay into a solid ball, and it sinks. Omar's team shapes the same mass of clay into a wide, hollow boat, and it floats. Explain why the boat floats but the ball sinks.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the boat shape pushes aside (displaces) more water, so the upthrust is bigger / big enough to balance the weight (the ball's upthrust is smaller than its weight). Accept: the shape is different, so the upward push of the water is bigger. Do not accept 'the boat is lighter' (the mass is the same) or 'the boat has air so it has less mass'.
questions.e: The mass, and so the weight, is the same. The wide hollow **shape** pushes aside much more water, so the **upthrust** on the boat is bigger — big enough to balance its weight. The small ball pushes aside only a little water, so its upthrust is smaller than its weight and it sinks. Shape, as well as mass, affects floating.

questions.q: (b) What is the name for the change in direction of light when it passes from one material into another?
questions.e: **Refraction.** Light changes direction (bends) as it passes between transparent materials such as water, glass and air.

questions.q: (d) Rana wants to add a second, identical lamp so that, when the switch is closed, **each** lamp is as bright as lamp R would be on its own. How should she connect the new lamp?
c: in series with lamp R
in parallel with lamp R
in place of the battery
across the open switch
questions.e: In a **parallel** circuit each lamp is connected directly across the battery, so each lamp is as bright as one lamp on its own. In series, two lamps share the push of the battery and are both dimmer.

Question 7
Ali lives on a farm in the Nile Delta. He grows bean plants in pots of three different soils from the farm: sandy soil, clay soil and loam (a mixture of sand, clay and humus). He grows four plants in each soil and measures their heights after three weeks. The bar chart shows the mean height for each soil.
questions.q: (d) Explain why the plants grew least well in the sandy soil.
questions.ms: Any two, 1 mark each: sandy soil has large particles / large spaces, so water drains through quickly; it holds (keeps) little water for the roots; it has little humus / organic matter; so it has few nutrients (minerals) for the plants. Do not accept 'sandy soil has no air' or 'it is too heavy'.
questions.e: Model answer: "Sandy soil has **large particles with big spaces** between them, so **water drains away quickly** and the roots get little water. It also has **little humus**, so it has **few nutrients** for the plants." Loam grew the best plants because it holds water but still drains, and the humus gives nutrients.

Question 7
Ali lives on a farm in the Nile Delta. He grows bean plants in pots of three different soils from the farm: sandy soil, clay soil and loam (a mixture of sand, clay and humus). He grows four plants in each soil and measures their heights after three weeks. The bar chart shows the mean height for each soil.
questions.q: (e) Ali wants to grow beans in the sandy soil next year. Which change would most help the plants to grow?
c: Mix in compost (humus) to the sandy soil.
Add more sand to the soil.
Remove all the small stones and humus.
Press the soil down hard so that no air is left.
questions.e: Adding **compost** (organic matter) changes the soil's composition: humus holds water like a sponge and adds nutrients, so it **supports** plant growth. Adding sand or removing humus would make it worse; pressing out the air **hinders** roots.

questions.p:
Question 9
Laila's night sky observation log also records three planets that she saw from Egypt: Venus, Mars and Jupiter.
questions.q: (a) Which sentence correctly describes the movements in our Solar System?
c: The Sun and the planets orbit the Earth.
The Moon orbits the Sun, and the Earth stays still.
The planets orbit the Moon, and the Moon orbits the Sun.
The planets orbit the Sun, and the Moon orbits the Earth.
questions.e: The **Sun is at the centre**. The eight planets, including Earth, **orbit the Sun**, and the **Moon orbits the Earth**. The Earth also spins on its axis, which gives us day and night.

questions.p:
Question 9
Laila's night sky observation log also records three planets that she saw from Egypt: Venus, Mars and Jupiter.
questions.q: (b) Which of the three planets in Laila's log is **closest** to the Sun?
questions.e: The order of the planets from the Sun is Mercury, **Venus**, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. So Venus is the closest of the three.

questions.p:
Question 9
Laila's night sky observation log also records three planets that she saw from Egypt: Venus, Mars and Jupiter.
questions.q: (c) Which planet in Laila's log has its orbit between the orbit of the Earth and the orbit of Jupiter?
questions.e: From the Sun: Earth (3rd), **Mars** (4th), Jupiter (5th). So Mars orbits between the Earth and Jupiter.

questions.p:
Question 10
Dad cooks pasta in a pan of salty water on the cooker in the family kitchen.
questions.q: (a) The water in the pan boils. Which sentence describes **boiling** but **not** evaporation?
c: The liquid changes into a gas.
It only happens at the surface of the liquid.
Bubbles of gas form all through the liquid, at one temperature.
It can happen at any temperature.
questions.e: In **boiling**, bubbles of gas form **throughout** the liquid, and it happens only at the **boiling point**. Evaporation happens only at the **surface** and at **any** temperature. Both change a liquid into a gas, so option A describes both.

questions.p:
Question 10
Dad cooks pasta in a pan of salty water on the cooker in the family kitchen.
questions.q: (b) After dinner, Dad wipes the worktop with a wet cloth. One hour later the worktop is dry, even though the water never got hot enough to boil. Name the process that dried the worktop.
questions.e: **Evaporation.** Water particles at the surface escape into the air as water vapour, even at room temperature.

Dad reads that 36 g of salt can dissolve in 100 ml of water at 20 °C, and 39 g can dissolve in 100 ml of water at 100 °C.
questions.q: (c) How many more grams of salt can dissolve in 100 ml of water at 100 °C than at 20 °C?
questions.e: 39 − 36 = **3 g**. More salt can dissolve in hot water than in cold water.

questions.q: (d) Dad notices that salt dissolves **faster** in hot water than in cold water. Use the particle model to explain why.
questions.ms: 1 mark: in hot water the (water) particles have more energy / move faster. 1 mark: so they hit (collide with) the salt more often / harder, pulling the salt particles away and spreading them out between the water particles more quickly. Do not accept 'the salt melts' or 'heat makes the salt disappear'.
questions.e: Model answer: "In hot water the **water particles move faster** (they have more energy). They **hit the salt crystals more often and harder**, so salt particles break away and **spread out between the water particles** more quickly." Remember: the salt dissolves; it does not melt.

questions.p:
Question 11
The family is getting ready for a party in the kitchen.
questions.q: (a) Hana ties two blown-up balloons to the ends of a stick. She hangs the stick from a string so that it balances. Then she pops one balloon. What happens?
c: The stick stays balanced, because air has no mass.
The end with the popped balloon goes down.
The end with the full balloon goes down, because the air in it has mass.
Both ends go up.
questions.e: When the balloon is popped, the air inside it escapes. The full balloon still has its squashed air inside, so that end is now heavier and **goes down**. This shows that **air (a gas) has mass**.

questions.p:
Question 11
The family is getting ready for a party in the kitchen.
questions.q: (b) Hana puts four spoons into cups of hot tea. Which spoon will feel hot fastest when she touches its handle?
c: a steel spoon
a wooden spoon
a plastic spoon
a bamboo spoon
questions.e: Metals such as **steel** are good **thermal conductors**: heat travels through them quickly, so the handle soon feels hot. Wood, plastic and bamboo are poor thermal conductors (thermal insulators). Metals are also good electrical conductors — conductivity is a property of a substance.
